title: Your January Returns Queue Gets Decided in October
summary: Returns get decided in October and invoiced in January. How to set carrier, visibility, refund timing, and January staffing in the fall.
body_markdown:
Almost every line on a peak worry list bills you in the same quarter it worries you.


When we ran our[2026 Peak Readiness Index](https://www.easypost.com/peak-season-shipping-statistics/) , a survey of 141 verified logistics professionals fielded in June, 9% named returns and reverse logistics their top peak concern. That put it fifth on a list of eight, behind shipping costs at 29%, forecasting at 21%, and carrier management at 20%.


I’m not going to argue those nine percent should have been ninety. What I’d point out is that returns are the only thing on that list where the money leaves in a different quarter from the decisions that set it. Surcharges land in December, and you fight them in December. Carrier capacity breaks in December, and you feel it that week. Returns get decided in October and invoiced in January, and almost nothing about how a company runs peak is built for that gap.


##


Nobody staffs the back half


The returns wave is difficult because of when it lands.


Outbound volume crests and falls off in the week before Christmas, and everybody exhales. The war room stops meeting, the seasonal hires finish their last shifts, and somebody sends a nice note about how well the team did.


Then reverse volume starts showing up, into a building running at normal December-30th headcount, carrying the output of a quarter that ran at three times normal.


I’d want that on a whiteboard in October. Not because returns spike after the holidays, which every operator already knows, but because the spike arrives at the exact moment you’ve released the capacity you’d need for it. You released it for good reasons, against a forecast that did its job. The forecast just stopped at delivery, the way most of them do.


##


The only cost that bills you next quarter


Look at what returns actually cost you and when.


The label is cheap and it’s paid in January. The labor to receive, inspect, and restock is paid in January. The refund is paid in January. And the customer decision, the one where somebody decides whether you’re worth a second order, gets made in January too.


Every input to those four things was locked in the fall. Which carrier and service you put on the[return label](https://www.easypost.com/returns/) . Whether anyone can see the package coming back. When the refund fires. How many people are on shift the first week of the year.


Our visibility data says most teams aren’t watching that gap close. Among the 115 shippers we asked, 10% named returns costs as the area where they can see the least. That’s fifth of seven, so it isn’t a crisis reading. It’s just consistent with a cost nobody is looking at in the quarter when it’s still changeable.


##


That queue is full of customers you just bought


Here’s the calculation I’d rather you run than take from me.


The people sending packages back in January are disproportionately the ones you acquired in November and early December, in the most expensive stretch of the year to acquire anybody. Plenty of them bought once. A good number received a gift, which means the person standing in your returns flow never chose you at all.


That flow is the only real interaction most of them will have with your operation beyond a box arriving. It’s an audition. By January the returns queue usually belongs to whoever is still on shift, and I’m not throwing stones at that, because it’s a rational place for a tired team to end up.


The comparison you pick decides the answer. Measure your returns process against the cost of processing a return and it looks like an efficiency question, which will always lose to something louder. Measure it against what you paid to acquire that customer in November, and it stops being an efficiency question.


Run rough numbers on your own operation. Say peak acquisition runs you $45 a customer, 15% of them return something, and your contribution margin on a repeat order is $30. On 10,000 peak orders, that’s 1,500 people in your returns queue, and roughly $67,500 of acquisition cost sitting in it. Lose an extra one in ten of them to a bad experience and you’ve given back 150 repeat orders. Those are made-up inputs; yours will be different, and that’s the point. Most teams have never put any number against that queue at all.


Speed is the lever you control.[QALO](https://www.easypost.com/case-studies/qalo) cut exchange turnaround from 7 to 14 days down to 2 to 5, on a return rate that reaches 10%. Their case study reports the turnaround and not a retention figure, so I won’t hand you a lift number I don’t have. Somewhere between five days and fourteen is the point where your customer stops waiting and buys the replacement elsewhere, and you can locate that point for your catalog better than I can.


### See where you sit going into peak


The 2026 Peak Readiness Index reports what 141 logistics professionals said about cost, carriers, and visibility heading into Q4, including the answers nobody quoted.


[Read the full Index →](https://learn.easypost.com/peak-2026-readiness-index-report)


##


Same shipment, half the instruments


You know where an outbound package is, what it’s going to cost, and whether the customer has heard anything about it. You know all three because you spent years making sure you would.


Coming back, most teams have a label and then nothing.


It’s the same shipment on the same carrier network, moving between the same two addresses, fully instrumented one way and dark the other, at the moment the customer is least happy with you and most likely to decide something permanent about whether to do this again.


Our own data points at that window without naming returns at all. Among those same 115 shippers, 21% said package delivery and the consumer experience is where they can see the least, tied for second with consumer demand and two points behind all-in cost. The post-purchase window is already a known blind spot. The reverse leg is the darkest corner of it.


On the forward trip, EasyPost Track customers see[61% fewer WISMO inquiries](https://www.easypost.com/products/track) . That’s a forward-leg number about our own product and I won’t dress it up as a returns statistic. It’s the benchmark for what the reverse trip is going without.


##


Make these three calls in the fall


None of these take long. All of them get made in the fall, by you or by default.


**What you’re buying on the return trip, cost or days.** Most returns go out on one service on one carrier, picked once, never revisited. A return has a weight, a zone, and a service level like anything else you ship, and the cheapest return service is almost always the slowest one. On a $30 shirt, slow is fine. On a $400 jacket where the customer is waiting to reorder the right size, those extra days are the thing costing you the second sale. Decide which shipments you’re buying speed for instead of inheriting one answer for all of them.


**What the customer can see while it’s coming back.** If I could only get you to do one of these three, it would be this one. This is the loop the last section opened. Tracking and status on the reverse leg is the cheapest thing on this list and the one most teams skip, and the silence it leaves generates the support ticket you were trying to avoid, in the week your team has the least room to answer it.


**When the refund fires.** On receipt scan, or on inspection. That one choice sets your cash exposure against your customer’s patience. Scan is faster and friendlier and exposes you to fraud and to returns that show up damaged. Inspection protects margin and costs you days you might not have. Finance and CX should have that conversation in November rather than discovering in January which one the platform picked for them.


Not all of it applies. If your catalog doesn’t generate exchanges, skip most of this rather than standing up a reverse-logistics program you don’t need. If you’re a 3PL, you inherit your clients’ returns terms and absorb their January volume without controlling either, so the useful move is pricing the back half into the contract instead of discovering it in the first week of the year.


##


What January costs, either way


Peak sends a second bill. It’s made of refunds, exchange cycles, restocking labor, and customers who bought exactly once, and it arrives in January against decisions taken in October by people watching outbound, because outbound was on fire.


The one thing I’d add to your October list is a headcount question, since it’s the one that can’t be fixed later. Somebody should decide, on purpose and with a number in front of them, who is working the first full week of January. Plenty of operations will look at that volume and conclude they can absorb it at normal staffing, and they’ll be right. It’s a much better answer when it was a decision.
